The blood pressure being high on the right side could be due to increased afterload because the left ventricle has to work harder to pump blood through the narrowed aorta.

Another possibility is coarctation of the aorta. This is a narrowing of the aorta, usually just after the aortic valve. It can cause high blood pressure in the upper extremities (like the right arm) because blood has to push through the narrowed area. The weak femoral pulses would make sense because the blood can't reach the lower extremities as well. However, coarctation typically presents with a murmur in the chest and back, often heard along the left sternal border, which aligns with the case. But in coarctation, the ejection click isn't usually present; it's more about the pressure gradient causing the murmur.

So, the presence of both a systolic murmur and an ejection click points more towards aortic stenosis. In aortic stenosis, the ejection click is due to the valve leaflets coming together during ejection, and the murmur is from the turbulent flow across the stenotic valve. The blood pressure being elevated on the right side could be due to the increased afterload causing the left ventricle to hypertrophy over time.

Another thought is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but that usually presents with an asymmetric septal hypertrophy and different murmurs. Plus, the ejection click isn't typically associated with that.

Putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is aortic stenosis. The elevated blood pressure, weak femoral pulses, and the specific heart sounds all point towards this condition. I think that's the best fit here.
